questions.title: Management of traumatic tympanic membrane perforation
questions.question: A 17-year-old male suffered a blow to the right side of the head by a blunt object, then noticed a few drops of blood from the right ear with diminished hearing. Examination shows a perforation of the right tympanic membrane with ragged, irregular edges and surrounding blood clots. Management of this case is:

options.A: Nothing per ear (keep water out of the ear) until spontaneous healing
options.B: Ear wash to remove any blood clots or debris

explanations.A: Correct. Most traumatic tympanic membrane perforations heal spontaneously within a few weeks if the ear is kept dry and free of infection. The essential management is to keep water and instruments out of the ear canal and to avoid ear drops or syringing, which introduce infection and displace the healing edges. Only a perforation that fails to heal after adequate time is later considered for myringoplasty.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ear washing or syringing forces water and organisms through the perforation into the middle ear and risks converting a clean traumatic perforation into a suppurative otitis media.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A hearing aid treats a fixed hearing loss, not an acute traumatic perforation that is expected to heal on its own with restoration of hearing.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Myringoplasty is reserved for a persistent perforation that has failed to heal; it is not done immediately, when spontaneous closure is the rule.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Exploration under general anaesthesia is not indicated for a simple traumatic perforation with no ossicular or facial-nerve injury.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that traumatic tympanic membrane perforations are managed by keeping the ear dry and allowing spontaneous healing.

questions.title: Features of a traumatic ear-drum perforation
questions.question: Traumatic ear-drum perforation is:

options.B: Usually a central perforation in the pars tensa

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer. Bleeding per ear is a true feature, but it is not the only correct statement, so it does not capture the full picture.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer. A traumatic perforation is indeed usually central in the pars tensa, but this is only one of several true statements.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer. Irregular (ragged) edges are characteristic, yet this too is only one true feature.
explanations.D: Correct. A traumatic tympanic membrane perforation typically bleeds a little into the canal, lies centrally in the pars tensa, and has irregular ragged edges often surrounded by blood clots. Because each of the three preceding statements is individually true, the complete answer is all of the above. These features together distinguish a fresh traumatic perforation from the marginal, non-bleeding perforations of chronic disease.

questions.learning_objective: List the features of a traumatic tympanic membrane perforation: bleeding per ear, central pars-tensa site and irregular edges.

questions.title: Treatment of auricular haematoma
questions.question: Treatment of auricular haematoma is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The pinna cartilage is not excised; excision would deform the auricle and is not the treatment of a collection of blood.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cautery has no role; the problem is a blood collection between perichondrium and cartilage, not bleeding to be cauterised.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tympanoplasty is a middle-ear/ear-drum reconstruction and is unrelated to a haematoma of the pinna.
explanations.D: Correct. An auricular haematoma is drained promptly by incision and evacuation of the clot, followed by a pressure dressing to prevent re-accumulation. Evacuation restores contact between the perichondrium and cartilage, preserving the cartilage's blood supply. If it is left undrained the cartilage is deprived of nutrition and fibroses, producing the deformed cauliflower ear.

questions.learning_objective: State that an auricular haematoma is treated by incision and evacuation with a pressure dressing to prevent cauliflower ear.

questions.title: Characteristic of a traumatic tympanic membrane perforation
questions.question: Traumatic perforation of the tympanic membrane is characterized by:

explanations.A: Correct. A traumatic perforation has irregular, ragged edges, often with blood clots at the margin, because the drum is torn rather than eroded by disease. It is typically central in the pars tensa and dry apart from a little blood. This contrasts with the smooth or marginal perforations and active discharge of chronic suppurative otitis media.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Purulent discharge indicates infection (suppurative otitis media), not a fresh traumatic tear.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An attic (pars flaccida) perforation is the hallmark of unsafe cholesteatomatous disease, not of trauma.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Congested middle-ear mucosa reflects active middle-ear inflammation, not an uncomplicated traumatic perforation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify irregular edges as the characteristic feature of a traumatic tympanic membrane perforation.

questions.title: Traumatic drum perforation — the exception
questions.question: Characteristics of a traumatic drum perforation include the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a true feature). Traumatic perforations have irregular edges, so it is not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is a true feature). The edges are thin and are often surrounded by blood clots.
explanations.C: Correct. Marginal is the exception: a traumatic perforation is central in the pars tensa, not marginal. Marginal perforations reach the annulus and are characteristic of unsafe chronic disease with cholesteatoma. Calling a traumatic perforation marginal is therefore the false statement in this list.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is a true feature). Because the injury is mechanical and uninfected, the middle-ear mucosa is normal.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that a traumatic perforation is central (not marginal), with irregular thin edges and normal middle-ear mucosa.

questions.title: Watery ear discharge increased by straining
questions.question: A watery ear discharge that increases by straining is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Serous (secretory) otitis media is a middle-ear effusion behind an intact drum; it does not discharge a watery fluid that varies with straining.
explanations.B: Correct. A clear, watery discharge from the ear that increases on straining, coughing or bending is cerebrospinal fluid otorrhoea, driven by the rise in CSF pressure these manoeuvres cause. It follows a breach of the dura and the temporal bone, usually after trauma or surgery, and can be confirmed by testing the fluid for beta-2 transferrin. Recognising it matters because it signals a communication with the subarachnoid space and a risk of meningitis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acute otitis media discharges mucopurulent, not clear watery, fluid and is not pressure-dependent in this way.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Malignant otitis externa produces a purulent, often granulation-associated discharge in an elderly diabetic, not a clear watery leak that changes with straining.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a clear watery ear discharge that increases on straining as CSF otorrhoea.

questions.title: Cause of pulsatile tinnitus
questions.question: Pulsatile tinnitus in the ear is due to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Malignant otitis externa causes deep otalgia and discharge, not a pulse-synchronous tinnitus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An osteoma is a benign bony canal swelling and does not generate a vascular pulsatile sound.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mastoiditis presents with post-auricular pain, swelling and fever, not pulsatile tinnitus.
explanations.D: Correct. Pulsatile tinnitus that is synchronous with the heartbeat points to a vascular middle-ear lesion, classically a glomus (paraganglioma) tumour. A glomus jugulare or glomus tympanicum shows as a red, pulsatile retrotympanic mass and produces a rising-sun or drum sign on otoscopy. Its rich vascular supply transmits the arterial pulse to the ear, generating the pulsatile character.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute pulsatile tinnitus with a vascular retrotympanic mass to a glomus jugulare tumour.

questions.title: Commonest presenting symptom of acoustic neuroma
questions.question: The commonest presenting symptom of acoustic neuroma is:

options.A: Unilateral tinnitus with progressive sensorineural hearing loss
options.D: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss with tinnitus

explanations.A: Correct. Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) most often presents with unilateral tinnitus and a slowly progressive sensorineural hearing loss, because the tumour arises on the vestibulocochlear nerve in the internal auditory canal. Any adult with asymmetric or unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus should be investigated for it, typically with MRI. The insidious cochlear symptoms come long before balance or cranial-nerve signs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Although the tumour is on the vestibular nerve, slow growth allows central compensation, so frank vertigo is uncommon and not the usual presenting complaint.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Facial and trigeminal involvement are late features of a large tumour compressing adjacent nerves, not the commonest presentation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sudden sensorineural hearing loss can occur but is far less common than the slowly progressive unilateral loss with tinnitus.

questions.learning_objective: State that acoustic neuroma commonly presents with unilateral tinnitus and progressive sensorineural hearing loss.

questions.title: Investigations in malignant otitis externa
questions.question: Investigations in malignant otitis externa include:

options.A: CT and MRI of the petrous bone
options.C: Radioactive isotope bone scan such as technetium and gallium
options.D: Culture and sensitivity of the ear discharge

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer. CT and MRI of the petrous bone assess bony erosion and soft-tissue/intracranial spread, but they are only one part of the work-up.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer. Blood sugar (the patient is usually diabetic) and ESR are needed, but again this is only one component.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer. Technetium and gallium scans detect osteomyelitis and are useful for monitoring, yet they do not stand alone.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the single best answer. Culture and sensitivity of the discharge guides antibiotic choice against Pseudomonas, but it is one of several needed tests.
explanations.E: Correct. Malignant (necrotising) otitis externa is a skull-base osteomyelitis, so it is investigated on several fronts at once: CT and MRI petrous for bony and soft-tissue extent, blood sugar and ESR to confirm the diabetic/inflammatory background, technetium and gallium isotope scans to demonstrate and follow the osteomyelitis, and culture and sensitivity of the discharge to direct anti-pseudomonal therapy. Because every listed investigation is appropriate, all of the above is the complete answer.

questions.learning_objective: List the investigations used in malignant otitis externa: CT/MRI petrous, blood sugar and ESR, isotope bone scan, and discharge culture.

questions.title: Ear canal full of white debris with black spots
questions.question: A 19-year-old male presents complaining of itching in the ear. On examination the canal is full of white debris with blackish spots. The diagnosis is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Malignant otitis externa is a severe skull-base infection of elderly diabetics with deep pain and granulations, not itching with fungal debris in a healthy young man.
explanations.B: Correct. Itching with a canal full of whitish debris studded with blackish spots is the classic picture of otomycosis, a fungal external otitis. The black spots are the conidiophores of Aspergillus niger, the commonest cause, embedded in the wet cotton-wool mycelium. Itching (rather than severe pain) is the dominant symptom, which fits this young patient.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acute otitis media is a middle-ear infection behind an intact drum, causing pain and fever, not canal debris with black spots.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Referred otalgia is pain from a distant site with a normal ear examination; it does not produce fungal debris.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Acute mastoiditis presents with post-auricular swelling and fever, not itching and canal debris.

questions.learning_objective: Diagnose otomycosis from itching and a canal full of white debris with blackish (Aspergillus) spots.

questions.title: Features of malignant otitis externa
questions.question: In malignant otitis externa:

options.B: The patient is diabetic with low immunity
options.C: The pathology is microangiopathy leading to osteomyelitis of the skull base

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is indeed the causative organism, but it is only one true statement.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer. The typical patient is an elderly diabetic or immunocompromised person, yet this is one feature among several.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer. The diabetic microangiopathy of the canal that progresses to skull-base osteomyelitis is correct, but not the whole answer.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the single best answer. Anti-pseudomonal quinolones (e.g. ciprofloxacin) are the mainstay of treatment, but this too is one item.
explanations.E: Correct. Malignant (necrotising) otitis externa is a Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection of the elderly diabetic or immunocompromised, in whom small-vessel disease of the canal allows the infection to spread to the temporal bone and skull base as osteomyelitis, and it is treated with prolonged anti-pseudomonal antibiotics such as quinolones. Because each statement is true, all of the above is the complete answer. Together they explain why the condition is aggressive and needs long systemic therapy.

questions.learning_objective: State that malignant otitis externa is a Pseudomonas skull-base osteomyelitis of the diabetic/immunocompromised treated with quinolones.

questions.title: True statement about otomycosis
questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding otomycosis is true?

options.B: It is treated by local antifungal ear drops
options.C: Invasive fungal infections are common in immunocompetent patients
options.D: The most common complaint is severe otalgia

explanations.A: Incorrect. Uncomplicated otomycosis is a superficial infection of the canal and does not need systemic antifungals.
explanations.B: Correct. Otomycosis is managed by thorough aural toilet to remove the fungal debris followed by topical antifungal ear drops such as clotrimazole, keeping the ear dry. Systemic antifungals are reserved for the rare invasive infection in an immunocompromised host. Local treatment with meticulous cleaning is therefore the true statement.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Invasive fungal infection occurs in the immunocompromised, not in immunocompetent patients, in whom disease stays superficial.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The dominant complaint is itching (with a sense of blockage), not severe otalgia.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that otomycosis is treated with aural toilet and topical antifungal ear drops.

questions.title: Otomycosis is another name for
questions.question: Otomycosis is another name for:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bacterial otitis externa (e.g. Pseudomonas or Staphylococcus) is a different entity from otomycosis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Viral otitis externa (such as herpes zoster oticus) is not what otomycosis means.
explanations.C: Correct. Otomycosis is by definition a fungal infection of the external auditory canal, that is, fungal otitis externa. The usual organisms are Aspergillus (commonest) and Candida. Naming it fungal otitis externa captures both the site (external canal) and the fungal aetiology.
explanations.D: Incorrect. One option (fungal otitis externa) is exactly correct, so none of the above is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Define otomycosis as fungal otitis externa.

questions.title: Uncontrolled diabetes in the elderly predisposes to
questions.question: Uncontrolled diabetes in an elderly patient may predispose to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cholesteatoma arises from retraction or migration of squamous epithelium into the middle ear and is not caused by diabetes.
explanations.B: Correct. Uncontrolled diabetes in an elderly patient is the classic predisposing background for malignant (necrotising) otitis externa. Diabetic small-vessel disease and impaired immunity let Pseudomonas infection of the canal spread to the temporal bone and skull base. This is why any elderly diabetic with persistent severe otalgia and granulations in the canal must be taken seriously.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Meniere's disease is an idiopathic endolymphatic hydrops, unrelated to diabetic control.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vestibular neuronitis is a post-viral vestibular disorder, not a complication of diabetes.

questions.learning_objective: Link uncontrolled diabetes in the elderly to malignant otitis externa.

questions.title: Main symptom of otomycosis
questions.question: The main symptom of otomycosis is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pain may occur if the canal is inflamed or macerated, but it is not the dominant complaint.
explanations.B: Incorrect. There is fungal debris rather than a true copious discharge, and discharge is not the leading symptom.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hearing loss is only mild and conductive if debris blocks the canal, not the main complaint.
explanations.D: Correct. Itching (pruritus) is the characteristic and dominant symptom of otomycosis, reflecting the superficial fungal colonisation of the canal skin. Patients often also feel blockage or fullness, but the itch is what brings them in. This helps separate it clinically from the painful bacterial otitis externa.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Vertigo is a labyrinthine symptom and has no part in a superficial fungal canal infection.

questions.learning_objective: Identify itching as the main symptom of otomycosis.

questions.title: Management of malignant otitis externa
questions.question: The management of malignant otitis externa includes:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer. Controlling the diabetes is essential but is only part of the management.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Radiotherapy has no role: despite its name, malignant otitis externa is an infection (skull-base osteomyelitis), not a tumour.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer. Large-dose prolonged anti-pseudomonal antibiotics are the mainstay, but this is only one component.
explanations.D: Incorrect. All of the above is wrong because it would include radiotherapy, which is not used.
explanations.E: Correct. Management combines strict control of the diabetes (A) with prolonged high-dose anti-pseudomonal antibiotics (C), plus local aural toilet and sometimes surgical debridement. Radiotherapy is explicitly not part of treatment because the condition is infective, not neoplastic. The best answer is therefore A and C together.

questions.learning_objective: State that malignant otitis externa is managed by controlling diabetes and giving large-dose antibiotics, not radiotherapy.

questions.title: Bacterial inflammation of the external auditory canal — the exception
questions.question: Bacterial inflammation of the external auditory canal can produce the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a bacterial condition). Furunculosis is a staphylococcal infection of a hair follicle in the outer canal, so it is produced by bacteria.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is a bacterial condition). Diffuse otitis externa is a spreading bacterial infection of the canal skin, commonly Pseudomonas.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is a bacterial condition). Malignant necrotising otitis externa is a Pseudomonas skull-base osteomyelitis, a bacterial disease.
explanations.D: Correct. Otomycosis is the exception because it is a fungal, not a bacterial, infection of the external canal, caused by Aspergillus or Candida. The other three (furunculosis, diffuse otitis externa and malignant necrotising otitis externa) are all bacterial. So the one condition not produced by bacterial inflammation is otomycosis.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish otomycosis (fungal) from the bacterial causes of external-canal inflammation.

questions.title: Treatment of secretory otitis media
questions.question: Treatment of secretory otitis media is:

options.B: Medical treatment in the first 3 months

explanations.A: Incorrect. Myringoplasty repairs a persistent tympanic membrane perforation; in secretory otitis media the drum is intact and retracted, so there is nothing to graft.
explanations.B: Correct. Secretory otitis media is managed conservatively at first: most effusions resolve within about three months with treatment of the underlying nasal and adenoidal cause, autoinflation and watchful waiting. Only an effusion that persists beyond this period, with a significant hearing loss, is taken to surgery for myringotomy and ventilation-tube insertion, usually with adenoidectomy. So initial treatment is medical rather than surgical.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mastoidectomy is an operation for suppurative mastoid disease or cholesteatoma, not for a sterile middle-ear effusion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. There is an effective initial treatment — a period of medical management — so "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that secretory otitis media is treated medically for the first three months before considering ventilation tubes.

questions.title: Manifestations of tubotympanic CSOM
questions.question: Tubotympanic CSOM might be manifested by:

options.C: Intermittent profuse odorless mucopurulent ear discharge

explanations.A: Incorrect. A very offensive (foul) discharge indicates bone destruction and cholesteatoma, which belong to the atticoantral (unsafe) type, not the tubotympanic type.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A high incidence of intracranial complications is a feature of the unsafe atticoantral type; the tubotympanic type is the "safe" type.
explanations.C: Correct. Tubotympanic (safe) chronic suppurative otitis media typically presents with an intermittent, profuse, odourless mucopurulent discharge that flares with upper respiratory infection or water entry. The perforation is central and the middle-ear mucosa, not bone, is the source of the mucoid discharge. Because there is no bone erosion, the discharge is not foul and serious complications are uncommon.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An attic (marginal) perforation is the hallmark of the atticoantral type; the tubotympanic type has a central perforation.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the intermittent, profuse, odourless mucopurulent discharge of tubotympanic (safe) CSOM.

questions.title: Presentation of acute mastoiditis
questions.question: Acute mastoiditis may present by:

options.A: Sagging of the posterosuperior meatal wall
options.B: Exostosis of the external auditory canal
options.D: Granulations on the floor of external auditory meatus

explanations.A: Correct. Sagging of the posterosuperior wall of the deep bony meatus is a classic sign of acute mastoiditis. It results from periostitis and subperiosteal collection over the mastoid antrum, which pushes the posterosuperior meatal wall inward. Together with mastoid tenderness, a pinna pushed forward and pulsatile discharge, it signals that infection has broken out of the air-cell system.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Exostoses are benign bony swellings from repeated cold-water exposure and are unrelated to acute mastoid infection.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fungal debris indicates otomycosis of the external canal, not acute mastoiditis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Granulations on the floor of the deep meatus point to chronic disease such as malignant otitis externa; they are not a feature of acute mastoiditis, where the sagging is posterosuperior.

questions.learning_objective: Identify sagging of the posterosuperior meatal wall as a sign of acute mastoiditis.

questions.title: Intracranial complication of CSOM
questions.question: An intracranial complication of chronic suppurative otitis media is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Petrositis is an intratemporal (aural) complication within the petrous apex, not an intracranial one.
explanations.B: Correct. An extradural (extradural/perisinus) abscess is one of the intracranial complications of chronic suppurative otitis media, collecting between the eroded bone and the dura. Intracranial complications also include subdural abscess, meningitis, brain abscess and lateral sinus thrombosis. They are distinguished from the intratemporal complications such as mastoiditis, petrositis, labyrinthitis and facial palsy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mastoiditis is the prototypical intratemporal complication, confined to the mastoid air cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A labyrinthine (perilymph) fistula is an intratemporal complication eroding into the inner ear, not an intracranial one.

questions.learning_objective: Classify extradural abscess as an intracranial complication of CSOM, distinct from intratemporal complications.

questions.title: Management of acute otitis media in a child
questions.question: A 6-year-old boy was brought by his parents for progressive right ear pain of two days' duration, associated with fever and a runny nose. On examination the external canal was healthy, but the right tympanic membrane was obviously reddish. Management of this condition may include all the following EXCEPT:

options.D: MRI scan of the petrous bones to assess the extent of the disease
options.E: Myringotomy if not responsive to medical treatment

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is part of management). Acute suppurative otitis media in a child is treated with an appropriate systemic antibiotic to clear the middle-ear infection.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is part of management). Analgesia, both local and systemic, is given to relieve the severe otalgia.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is part of management). Antipyretics and general measures control the fever and discomfort.
explanations.D: Correct. Uncomplicated acute otitis media is a clinical diagnosis, and cross-sectional imaging such as an MRI of the petrous bones has no role in its routine management. Imaging is reserved for a suspected complication (for example mastoiditis or an intracranial spread), not for a simple red drum. Ordering it here would be unnecessary and is therefore the exception.
explanations.E: Incorrect (this is part of management). Myringotomy to drain the middle ear is done if the child fails to respond to medical treatment or the drum is bulging.

questions.learning_objective: State that routine management of acute otitis media does not include cross-sectional imaging of the petrous bones.

questions.title: Treatment of unsafe CSOM with cholesteatoma
questions.question: In unsafe CSOM (with cholesteatoma) the treatment of choice is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A simple (cortical) mastoidectomy clears the mastoid air cells but does not exteriorise the attic and antrum, so it leaves cholesteatoma behind.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A ventilation tube treats a middle-ear effusion; it has no place in eradicating cholesteatoma.
explanations.C: Correct. Unsafe (atticoantral) chronic suppurative otitis media with cholesteatoma is treated surgically, and the classic operation is a radical (or modified radical/canal-wall-down) mastoidectomy that removes all the cholesteatoma and exteriorises the diseased cavity. The overriding aim is to render the ear safe from intracranial and other complications. Hearing reconstruction is secondary to complete removal of disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tympanoplasty alone reconstructs the drum and ossicles but does not eradicate cholesteatoma from the attic and antrum.

questions.learning_objective: State that cholesteatoma (unsafe CSOM) is treated by radical mastoidectomy.

questions.title: Signs of acute mastoiditis — the exception
questions.question: Acute mastoiditis may present by any of the following EXCEPT:

options.A: Sagging of the posterosuperior meatal wall
options.D: Granulations on the floor of external auditory meatus

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a sign). Sagging of the posterosuperior meatal wall from subperiosteal collection over the antrum is a classic sign of acute mastoiditis.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a sign). The reservoir sign — immediate refilling of the meatus with pus after cleaning — reflects a mastoid reservoir discharging through the perforation.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a sign). Acute mastoiditis usually follows a perforation, and a perforation with pulsatile mucopurulent discharge is expected.
explanations.D: Correct. Granulations on the floor of the deep external auditory meatus are not a feature of acute mastoiditis; that finding points to malignant (necrotising) otitis externa or long-standing disease. In acute mastoiditis the wall change is a posterosuperior sagging, not floor granulations, so this option is the exception.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the true signs of acute mastoiditis from meatal-floor granulations.

questions.title: Characteristics of cholesteatoma
questions.question: Cholesteatoma is characterized by:

options.D: Erosion of the ossicles to cause conductive deafness

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer. A scanty, foul-smelling discharge is typical of cholesteatoma, but it is only one of its features.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer. A marginal (attic) perforation is characteristic, but again only one feature.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer. Cholesteatoma can erode bone and cause intracranial complications, but this too is one feature among several.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the single best answer. Erosion of the ossicular chain producing conductive deafness is characteristic, but not the whole picture.
explanations.E: Correct. Cholesteatoma is characterised by all of these: a scanty offensive discharge, a marginal/attic perforation, erosion of the ossicles causing conductive deafness, and the potential for bone destruction leading to intracranial complications. Because it destroys bone, it is the "unsafe" ear. All four statements are true, so "all of the above" is the best answer.

questions.learning_objective: List the characteristic features of cholesteatoma.

questions.title: Complications of otitis media — the exception
questions.question: Otitis media may be complicated by all of the following except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a complication). A brain (otogenic) abscess, usually temporal-lobe or cerebellar, is a recognised intracranial complication of otitis media.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a complication). Lateral (sigmoid) sinus thrombosis/thrombophlebitis is a classic intracranial complication.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a complication). A mastoid (subperiosteal) abscess is an intratemporal complication when infection breaks through the mastoid cortex.
explanations.D: Correct. A parapharyngeal abscess arises from tonsillar, pharyngeal or dental infection, not from the middle ear, so it is not a complication of otitis media. The genuine complications spread from the temporal bone — intratemporal (mastoiditis, petrositis, labyrinthitis, facial palsy) or intracranial (meningitis, brain abscess, sinus thrombosis). Parapharyngeal spread is therefore the exception.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that a parapharyngeal abscess is not a complication of otitis media.

questions.title: Indication for radical mastoidectomy
questions.question: Radical mastoidectomy is indicated in:

explanations.A: Correct. Radical mastoidectomy is indicated for extensive cholesteatoma (unsafe atticoantral disease), where the goal is to remove all disease and exteriorise the mastoid and middle ear into a single safe cavity. It is chosen when the disease cannot be cleared while preserving the canal wall. The priority is a safe, dry ear rather than hearing.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Otosclerosis is treated by stapedectomy or a hearing aid, not by mastoidectomy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Secretory otitis media is treated medically and, if persistent, by ventilation tubes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A traumatic drum perforation is managed by keeping the ear dry for spontaneous healing.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Tympanosclerosis is managed by hearing rehabilitation or tympanoplasty, not radical mastoidectomy.

questions.learning_objective: State that radical mastoidectomy is indicated for cholesteatoma.

questions.title: Commonest cause of hearing loss in a child
questions.question: The most common cause of diminution of hearing in a 5-year-old child is:

options.E: Traumatic rupture of the tympanic membrane

explanations.A: Correct. Bilateral middle-ear effusion (secretory otitis media, or "glue ear") is by far the commonest cause of acquired hearing loss in young children. Adenoid hypertrophy and Eustachian-tube dysfunction lead to a persistent sterile effusion that dampens sound conduction. It typically causes a mild-to-moderate conductive loss and may present as inattention or delayed speech.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Congenital deaf-mutism (severe sensorineural loss) is uncommon compared with glue ear and usually presents earlier, with absent speech development.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tympanosclerosis with ossicular fixation is a late sequel of chronic ear disease and is rare at this age.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Noise-induced hearing loss from loud sound is a problem of later life and repeated exposure, not a typical cause in a 5-year-old.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Traumatic drum rupture causes a sudden unilateral loss after a specific injury, not the usual chronic bilateral loss of childhood.

questions.learning_objective: Identify bilateral middle-ear effusion as the commonest cause of childhood hearing loss.

questions.title: Consequence of untreated tubotympanic CSOM
questions.question: A 35-year-old male presented with right ear discharge for five years. The discharge is intermittent and profuse. On examination the right external canal was full of muco-purulent discharge, and suction revealed a central kidney-shaped perforation in the ear drum. If this condition is left untreated, the most probable consequence will be:

options.B: Progressive hearing loss up to complete deafness
options.D: Spread of the infection to the intracranial cavity
options.E: Septicemia secondary to a septic focus in the ear

explanations.A: Incorrect. Repeated discharge is the ongoing picture of the disease, not the eventual consequence the question asks for.
explanations.B: Correct. This is tubotympanic (safe) chronic suppurative otitis media — a central perforation with mucopurulent discharge and no bone destruction. Left untreated it does not usually cause intracranial complications, but the persistent inflammation and ossicular damage lead to a progressive conductive hearing loss that can advance to severe deafness. So the most probable long-term consequence is worsening hearing.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Facial paralysis is a complication of the unsafe atticoantral (cholesteatoma) type with bone erosion, not of the safe central-perforation type.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Intracranial spread is characteristic of the unsafe type; the safe tubotympanic type rarely does this.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Septicaemia from an ear focus is not the expected outcome of safe CSOM.

questions.learning_objective: Predict progressive hearing loss as the consequence of untreated safe (tubotympanic) CSOM.

questions.title: Surgical treatment of persistent otitis media with effusion
questions.question: Otitis media with effusion in children, when it persists, is treated by:

options.A: Medical treatment in the form of systemic steroids for several weeks
options.B: Medical treatment in the form of systemic steroids only for 48 hours
options.D: Adenoidectomy and placement of ventilation tubes
options.E: Long term penicillin till the age of 15 years

explanations.A: Incorrect. Prolonged systemic steroids are not an accepted treatment for glue ear and carry needless risk.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A 48-hour course of steroids has no established role in resolving a persistent middle-ear effusion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A myringotomy alone drains the effusion but the fluid re-accumulates; without a ventilation tube the benefit is short-lived.
explanations.D: Correct. When otitis media with effusion persists beyond about three months with a significant hearing loss, the standard surgical treatment is myringotomy with insertion of ventilation tubes (grommets), commonly combined with adenoidectomy to remove the obstructing and infective focus. This ventilates the middle ear and restores hearing. Adenoidectomy with grommets is therefore the definitive procedure.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Long-term prophylactic penicillin is not used for glue ear and would not clear a sterile effusion.

questions.learning_objective: State that persistent otitis media with effusion is treated by adenoidectomy and ventilation tubes.

questions.title: Cranial complications of CSOM — the exception
questions.question: The following is a cranial (intratemporal) complication of CSOM except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS an intratemporal complication). Labyrinthitis is inflammation of the inner ear within the temporal bone.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS an intratemporal complication). Petrositis is infection of the petrous apex within the temporal bone.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS an intratemporal complication). Mastoiditis is confined to the mastoid air cells of the temporal bone.
explanations.D: Correct. A subdural abscess lies inside the cranial cavity between dura and arachnoid, so it is an intracranial — not an intratemporal — complication. The other three (labyrinthitis, petrositis, mastoiditis) are complications within the temporal bone. The subdural abscess is therefore the exception.

questions.learning_objective: Separate intratemporal complications of CSOM from the intracranial subdural abscess.

questions.title: Primary goal of cholesteatoma surgery
questions.question: The primary goal of surgery for cholesteatoma is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Improving hearing is a desirable secondary aim, achieved only after the ear is made safe.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ossicular reconstruction is part of hearing rehabilitation, not the primary objective.
explanations.C: Correct. The overriding aim of cholesteatoma surgery is complete removal (eradication) of the disease to obtain a safe, dry ear and prevent life-threatening complications. Because cholesteatoma erodes bone and can cause intracranial spread, clearing all of it takes priority over hearing. Reconstruction of hearing is addressed only once the disease is fully removed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Reconstructing the drum is part of later hearing reconstruction, again secondary to eradicating disease.

questions.learning_objective: State that the primary goal of cholesteatoma surgery is complete removal of disease.

questions.title: Commonest cause of bilateral conductive deafness in a child
questions.question: The most common cause of bilateral conductive deafness in a child is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Otosclerosis typically causes conductive deafness in young adults, not in children.
explanations.B: Correct. Secretory otitis media (glue ear) is the commonest cause of bilateral conductive deafness in children. A persistent middle-ear effusion, driven by adenoidal obstruction and Eustachian-tube dysfunction, impairs sound transmission across the ossicular chain. It is usually reversible once the effusion clears or is drained.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Congenital cholesteatoma is rare and usually unilateral.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adhesive otitis media is a later scarring sequel of long-standing effusion and is much less common than active glue ear.

questions.learning_objective: Identify secretory otitis media as the commonest cause of bilateral conductive deafness in children.

questions.title: Discharge in cholesteatoma
questions.question: Cholesteatoma is characterized by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A continuous mucopurulent discharge is the picture of tubotympanic (safe) disease from the middle-ear mucosa, not of cholesteatoma.
explanations.B: Correct. Cholesteatoma produces a scanty but characteristically foul-smelling (offensive) discharge, because keratin debris and bone erosion allow anaerobic infection. The odour reflects the bone destruction that defines the unsafe ear. This foul discharge, with a marginal/attic perforation, is a key clue to cholesteatoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cholesteatoma is associated with a marginal or attic perforation; a central perforation is the tubotympanic (safe) type.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A foul-smelling discharge is indeed characteristic, so "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the scanty foul-smelling discharge of cholesteatoma.

questions.title: Retracted drum after inadequately treated acute otitis media
questions.question: A child with a retracted drum and conductive deafness after inadequate treatment of acute suppurative otitis media is suffering from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chronic tubotympanic otitis media has a central perforation with active mucopurulent discharge, not an intact retracted drum.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Atticoantral disease has a marginal/attic perforation with cholesteatoma and a foul discharge, not a simply retracted intact drum.
explanations.C: Correct. A retracted, intact drum with conductive deafness following incompletely treated acute otitis media is otitis media with effusion (glue ear). The residual middle-ear fluid and negative pressure retract the drum and dampen hearing. There is no perforation, which separates it from the chronic suppurative types.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The picture fits otitis media with effusion, so "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Diagnose otitis media with effusion from a retracted intact drum with conductive loss.

questions.title: Features of tubotympanic CSOM — the exception
questions.question: All of the following may be seen in the tubotympanic type of chronic suppurative otitis media EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS seen). A mucopurulent otorrhoea from the middle-ear mucosa is typical of the tubotympanic type.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS seen). A central perforation is the defining feature of the tubotympanic (safe) type.
explanations.C: Correct. A marginal (attic) perforation is the hallmark of the atticoantral (unsafe) type, not the tubotympanic type. The tubotympanic type has a central perforation with the annulus intact. So a marginal perforation is the exception here.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS seen). The discharge in tubotympanic disease is characteristically intermittent and profuse.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that a marginal perforation is not a feature of tubotympanic CSOM.

questions.title: Features of secretory otitis media
questions.question: Secretory otitis media is characterized by:

options.C: It is predisposed to by enlarged adenoids

explanations.A: Incorrect. Secretory otitis media is predominantly a disease of children; a new unilateral effusion in an adult should instead raise suspicion of a nasopharyngeal mass.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A middle-ear effusion gives a flat type B (or negative-pressure type C) tympanogram, not the normal type A curve.
explanations.C: Correct. Enlarged adenoids are a major predisposing factor for secretory otitis media: they obstruct the Eustachian-tube opening and harbour infection, impairing middle-ear ventilation and drainage. The resulting negative pressure and effusion produce the conductive hearing loss. This is why adenoidectomy is part of surgical treatment.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Myringoplasty repairs a perforation; secretory otitis media has an intact drum and is treated medically or by ventilation tubes.

questions.learning_objective: Identify enlarged adenoids as a predisposing factor for secretory otitis media.

questions.title: Meniere's disease triad
questions.question: Recurrent attacks of vertigo, sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus is typically characteristic of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Vestibular neuronitis causes acute vertigo alone, without hearing loss or tinnitus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acoustic neuroma causes progressive unilateral sensorineural loss and tinnitus, but vertigo is usually mild and not the recurrent episodic attacks described.
explanations.C: Correct. Recurrent episodic vertigo with fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus (often with aural fullness) is the classic triad of Meniere's disease, caused by endolymphatic hydrops. The attacks last minutes to hours and recur over years. This episodic triad distinguishes it from the steady progression of an acoustic neuroma.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Congenital cholesteatoma presents with conductive hearing loss and an intact drum, not this vestibular triad.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the vertigo–SNHL–tinnitus triad of Meniere's disease.

questions.title: Signs of raised intracranial tension — the exception
questions.question: Signs of increased intracranial tension include all EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a sign). Headache, worse in the morning, is a cardinal symptom of raised intracranial pressure.
explanations.B: Correct. Neck stiffness is a sign of meningeal irritation (meningism), not of raised intracranial tension itself. The features of raised pressure are headache, vomiting and papilloedema with blurring of vision. Neck rigidity therefore points to meningitis rather than to the pressure rise, making it the exception.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a sign). Projectile or effortless vomiting accompanies raised intracranial pressure.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS a sign). Blurring of vision from papilloedema is a classic sign of raised intracranial pressure.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish signs of raised intracranial pressure from meningeal neck stiffness.

questions.title: Cranial complication of suppurative otitis media
questions.question: A cranial (intratemporal) complication of suppurative otitis media is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sphenoiditis is inflammation of the sphenoid sinus, a rhinological condition unrelated to otitis media.
explanations.B: Correct. Petrositis — infection spreading to the petrous apex of the temporal bone — is an intratemporal complication of suppurative otitis media. It classically produces Gradenigo's syndrome (ear discharge, deep facial/retro-orbital pain and sixth-nerve palsy with diplopia). Being within the temporal bone, it is grouped with mastoiditis and labyrinthitis rather than with the intracranial complications.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Encephalitis is not a recognised direct complication of otitis media; the intracranial spread produces meningitis or a brain abscess instead.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An extradural abscess is a genuine complication but an intracranial one, so it does not fit the intratemporal category asked for here.

questions.learning_objective: Classify petrositis as an intratemporal complication of suppurative otitis media.

questions.title: Commonest route of infection to the middle ear
questions.question: The most common route for infection to reach the middle ear is through:

options.A: Traumatic perforation of the tympanic membrane

explanations.A: Incorrect. Infection through a traumatic perforation (from outside in) is uncommon and requires a pre-existing hole in the drum.
explanations.B: Correct. The Eustachian tube is the usual route by which infection ascends from the nasopharynx to the middle ear, which is why otitis media so often follows an upper respiratory infection or adenoid disease. The tube is shorter, wider and more horizontal in children, explaining their higher incidence. Tubal spread of nasopharyngeal organisms is therefore the commonest route.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Blood-borne (haematogenous) infection of the middle ear is rare.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Retrograde spread from meningitis is unusual; more often infection travels from the ear to the meninges, not the reverse.

questions.learning_objective: State that the commonest route of middle-ear infection is the Eustachian tube.

questions.title: Treatment of mastoid abscess
questions.question: Mastoid abscess is treated by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A simple incision drains the pus but leaves the infected mastoid air cells, so the abscess recurs.
explanations.B: Correct. A mastoid (subperiosteal) abscess complicating acute mastoiditis is treated by cortical (simple) mastoidectomy, which exenterates the infected air cells and drains the antrum while preserving the middle-ear structures and canal wall. Antibiotics alone will not clear coalescent mastoid disease. Cortical mastoidectomy is therefore the operation of choice.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Radical mastoidectomy is reserved for cholesteatoma (unsafe disease), not for acute mastoid abscess.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tympanoplasty reconstructs the drum and ossicles; it does not drain an acute mastoid abscess.

questions.learning_objective: State that a mastoid abscess is treated by cortical mastoidectomy.

questions.title: Symptoms of CSOM — the exception
questions.question: All are symptoms of chronic suppurative otitis media EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a symptom). Ear discharge (otorrhoea) is the leading symptom of chronic suppurative otitis media.
explanations.B: Correct. Uncomplicated chronic suppurative otitis media is characteristically painless; the perforation vents the middle ear so pressure does not build up. The appearance of pain in a known CSOM is a warning sign of a developing complication such as mastoiditis or an intracranial abscess. So pain is the exception among its usual symptoms.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a symptom). A conductive hearing loss (deafness) is expected from the perforation and ossicular damage.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS a symptom). Tinnitus commonly accompanies the hearing loss.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that uncomplicated CSOM is painless and that pain suggests a complication.

questions.title: Vertigo with sensorineural hearing loss
questions.question: Vertigo with sensorineural hearing loss occurs in:

explanations.A: Correct. Labyrinthitis inflames the whole membranous labyrinth, so it affects both the vestibular apparatus (causing vertigo) and the cochlea (causing sensorineural hearing loss). The combination of vertigo with hearing loss localises the lesion to the labyrinth. This is what separates it from a purely vestibular disorder.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Vestibular neuritis affects only the vestibular nerve, giving vertigo with normal hearing.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cerebellar lesions cause imbalance and ataxia but not sensorineural hearing loss.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo causes brief positional vertigo with no hearing loss.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that vertigo combined with sensorineural hearing loss localises to labyrinthitis.

questions.title: Cranial complication of otitis media
questions.question: A cranial (intratemporal) complication of otitis media is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. External otitis is a disease of the outer ear canal, not a complication of middle-ear otitis media.
explanations.B: Correct. Petrositis, infection of the petrous temporal bone, is an intratemporal ("cranial") complication of otitis media. It shares this category with mastoiditis, labyrinthitis and facial palsy — all confined to the temporal bone. Brain abscess and lateral sinus thrombosis, by contrast, are intracranial complications.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A brain abscess is an intracranial complication, not an intratemporal one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lateral sinus thrombosis is likewise an intracranial complication.

questions.learning_objective: Classify petrositis as an intratemporal complication, separate from intracranial brain abscess and sinus thrombosis.

questions.title: Triad of otorrhoea, diplopia and facial pain
questions.question: Triad of ear discharge, diplopia and facial pain are symptoms of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acute mastoiditis gives post-auricular pain, swelling and a sagging meatal wall, not diplopia and facial pain.
explanations.B: Correct. The triad of ear discharge, diplopia (from a sixth-nerve palsy) and deep facial or retro-orbital pain (from fifth-nerve irritation) is Gradenigo's syndrome, which follows suppuration of the petrous apex, that is petrositis. The abducent nerve and the trigeminal ganglion lie close to the petrous apex, so infection there paralyses lateral eye movement and irritates the trigeminal nerve. Recognising this triad in a discharging ear signals that infection has reached the petrous apex.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A cerebellar abscess causes ataxia, nystagmus and signs of raised intracranial pressure, not this specific petrous-apex triad.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bezold's abscess is pus tracking into the neck below the mastoid tip, presenting as a tender neck swelling rather than diplopia.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise Gradenigo's triad of otorrhoea, diplopia and facial pain as petrositis.

questions.title: Intermittent (picket-fence) fever in ear disease
questions.question: Intermittent fever is seen in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. An otitic brain abscess typically gives a low-grade or normal temperature with headache and focal signs, not a swinging fever.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An extradural abscess is often silent or causes only a persistent headache and discharge, without the picket-fence fever.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bezold's abscess presents as a tender neck swelling from pus tracking below the mastoid tip, not a characteristic intermittent fever.
explanations.D: Correct. A swinging, intermittent (picket-fence) fever with rigors is characteristic of lateral (sigmoid) sinus thrombophlebitis complicating chronic ear disease, because septic emboli are showered into the blood stream from the infected thrombus. The temperature spikes as organisms are released, then falls, giving the hectic pattern. Blood cultures taken at the peak of the fever are often positive.

questions.learning_objective: Associate a swinging (picket-fence) fever in ear disease with lateral sinus thrombophlebitis.

questions.title: Predisposing factors of acute otitis media in infants (the exception)
questions.question: The predisposing factors of acute otitis media in infants include all the following EXCEPT:

options.A: Adenoiditis, tonsillitis and exanthemata are frequent in children
options.B: During teething with its associated rhinitis, gastroenteritis and artificial feeding
options.C: The longer, narrower and vertical Eustachian tube predisposes to infection
options.D: The contaminated milk may enter the Eustachian tube as a result of feeding in supine position

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a true factor). Frequent adenoiditis, tonsillitis and childhood exanthemata do predispose infants to acute otitis media.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is a true factor). Teething with its associated rhinitis and gastroenteritis, and artificial feeding, are recognised predisposing factors.
explanations.C: Correct. This statement is the exception because it reverses the truth: the infant Eustachian tube is in fact shorter, wider and more horizontal than in the adult, and it is this arrangement, not a longer, narrower, vertical tube, that lets nasopharyngeal infection and refluxed milk reach the middle ear easily. The other options are genuine predisposing factors. So the false statement is the one describing a longer, narrower, vertical tube.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is a true factor). Feeding a baby supine can let contaminated milk reflux up the Eustachian tube into the middle ear.

questions.learning_objective: State that the infant Eustachian tube is short, wide and horizontal, predisposing to acute otitis media.

questions.title: Cholesteatoma — the false statement
questions.question: Which statement about cholesteatoma is NOT true:

options.C: It can be treated with ear tube placement
options.D: It can cause facial paralysis and hearing loss

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is true). Cholesteatoma is often treated with mastoid surgery to remove the disease.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is true). By eroding into the cranial cavity it can cause life-threatening complications such as meningitis or brain abscess.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the untrue statement: cholesteatoma is an expanding, bone-eroding keratin sac that must be removed surgically (usually by mastoidectomy), and it cannot be treated by inserting a ventilation (grommet) ear tube. Ear tubes are used for a sterile middle-ear effusion, not for eradicating cholesteatoma. Managing cholesteatoma with a tube would let it keep destroying bone and cause complications.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is true). Erosion of the facial canal and the ossicles causes facial paralysis and hearing loss.
explanations.E: Incorrect (this is true). Cholesteatoma characteristically produces a marginal (attic) perforation.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that cholesteatoma requires surgical removal and cannot be treated with ventilation tubes.
