questions.title: What cholesteatoma is
questions.question: Cholesteatoma is:

options.B: An infected keratin-containing sac of the middle ear
options.C: A bony lesion that invaded the middle ear

explanations.A: Incorrect. It is not a true tumour (neoplasm), even though its name misleadingly ends in '-oma'.
explanations.B: Correct. Cholesteatoma is an infected sac of keratinising squamous epithelium (skin) trapped in the middle ear or attic and filled with desquamated keratin debris. Despite the name it is not a true neoplasm and not a primary bony lesion; it is a misplaced skin sac whose enzymes and expansile pressure erode surrounding bone. Calling it an infected keratin-containing sac captures both its epithelial nature and its tendency to suppurate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. It is not itself a bony lesion; it is a soft keratin sac that secondarily erodes bone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Because A and C are wrong, 'all of the above' cannot be correct.
explanations.E: Incorrect. One option (an infected keratin-containing sac) is exactly correct, so 'none of the above' is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Define cholesteatoma as an infected keratin-containing sac, not a true neoplasm.

questions.title: Nature and prognosis of Bell's palsy
questions.question: Bell's palsy:

options.A: Is an upper motor neuron palsy
options.B: Is a very rare cause of facial paralysis
options.C: Recovery is usual and spontaneous but may be incomplete

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bell’s palsy is a lower, not upper, motor neuron palsy, so it involves the whole half of the face.
explanations.B: Incorrect. It is in fact the commonest cause of facial paralysis, not a rare one.
explanations.C: Correct. Bell's palsy is an idiopathic lower motor neuron facial paralysis, and in most patients recovery is spontaneous and good, though a proportion are left with incomplete recovery or synkinesis. Because it is a lower motor neuron lesion it affects the whole side of the face and is not accompanied by limb weakness. A short early course of corticosteroids improves the chance of full recovery.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is an isolated facial nerve lesion; associated hemiplegia would indicate a central (stroke) cause instead.

questions.learning_objective: State that Bell's palsy is an idiopathic lower motor neuron facial palsy that usually recovers spontaneously.

questions.title: Commonest cause of facial paralysis
questions.question: Commonest cause of facial paralysis is:

explanations.A: Correct. Bell's palsy, the idiopathic lower motor neuron facial paralysis, is by far the commonest cause of facial nerve paralysis. It is a diagnosis of exclusion made once other causes such as trauma, infection and tumour have been ruled out. Its high frequency is why any acute isolated facial palsy is regarded as Bell's until proven otherwise.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Iatrogenic injury during mastoid or parotid surgery causes facial palsy but is far less common than Bell's palsy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Guillain-Barré syndrome can cause bilateral facial weakness but is a rare cause overall.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Trauma to the facial nerve is an important but much less frequent cause than Bell's palsy.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Bell’s palsy as the commonest cause of facial nerve paralysis.

questions.title: Which statement truly represents Bell's palsy
questions.question: Which one of the following statements truly represents Bell's palsy:

options.A: Hemiparesis and contralateral facial nerve paralysis
options.B: Combined paralysis of the facial, abducent and trigeminal nerves
options.C: Bilateral facial palsy due to congenital anomaly of the facial nerve
options.D: Idiopathic paralysis of the facial nerve that recovers completely in most cases
options.E: Facial nerve paralysis following ear surgery

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hemiparesis with contralateral facial weakness describes a central (upper motor neuron or stroke) lesion, not Bell’s palsy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Combined facial, abducent and trigeminal palsy suggests a petrous apex or skull-base lesion, not Bell’s palsy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bell’s palsy is acquired and idiopathic, not a congenital bilateral anomaly.
explanations.D: Correct. Bell's palsy is by definition an idiopathic (unknown-cause) lower motor neuron paralysis of the facial nerve, and in most patients it recovers completely. There is no limb weakness, no involvement of other cranial nerves and no preceding surgery, features that would each point to other diagnoses. This idiopathic, self-limiting nature is exactly what distinguishes Bell's palsy.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Palsy after ear surgery is iatrogenic trauma and by definition not idiopathic Bell’s palsy.

questions.learning_objective: Define Bell's palsy as an idiopathic facial nerve paralysis that recovers completely in most cases.

questions.title: Fibres present in the facial nerve (the exception)
questions.question: The following fibers are present in the facial nerve EXCEPT:

options.A: Secretomotor fibers to the lacrimal gland through the GSPN
options.B: Secretomotor fibers to the submandibular gland through the chorda tympani
options.C: Taste sensation fibers to the anterior third of the tongue through the chorda tympani
options.D: Motor fibers to the stapedius muscle
options.E: Motor fibers to the tensor tympani muscle

explanations.A: Incorrect (this fibre is present). The facial nerve gives secretomotor fibres to the lacrimal gland through the greater superficial petrosal nerve.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this fibre is present). Secretomotor fibres to the submandibular and sublingual glands run in the chorda tympani.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this fibre is present). Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue travels in the chorda tympani.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this fibre is present). The nerve to stapedius is a motor branch of the facial nerve.
explanations.E: Correct. This is the exception: the tensor tympani is supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, not by the facial nerve. The facial nerve does carry the other listed fibres, namely secretomotor to the lacrimal gland via the greater superficial petrosal nerve, secretomotor and taste fibres via the chorda tympani, and motor fibres to the stapedius. So motor supply to the tensor tympani is the fibre not found in the facial nerve.

questions.learning_objective: Recall that the facial nerve supplies stapedius but not tensor tympani, which is trigeminal.

questions.title: First-line treatment of facial palsy complicating acute otitis media
questions.question: The first line of treatment in a child who develops lower motor neuron facial paralysis after acute otitis media is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Corticosteroids are the treatment of idiopathic Bell’s palsy; when the cause is an infected middle ear the priority is to drain the pus, not to give steroids.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Formal facial nerve decompression is a later, second-line measure reserved for palsy that persists despite drainage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Exploration of the nerve is not the first step; drainage of the infected middle ear is.
explanations.D: Correct. Facial palsy that develops during acute otitis media is caused by pus under pressure in the middle ear irritating the nerve through a dehiscent facial canal, so the first-line treatment is urgent myringotomy to drain the middle ear together with intravenous antibiotics. Relieving the pus usually leads to rapid recovery of the nerve. Surgical decompression or exploration is reserved for the rare case that fails to improve after drainage.

questions.subtopic: Facial palsy in acute otitis media
questions.learning_objective: State that facial palsy complicating acute otitis media is first treated by urgent myringotomy and antibiotics.

questions.title: Features of lower motor neuron facial paralysis
questions.question: Lower motor neuron facial paralysis is characterized by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hyper-reflexia is a feature of an upper motor neuron lesion, not a lower motor neuron one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Preserved emotional (mimetic) movement is seen in upper motor neuron lesions; in a lower motor neuron palsy all movement of that side is lost.
explanations.C: Correct. A lower motor neuron facial palsy denervates the muscles of facial expression, so over time they show wasting and, on electrical testing, degeneration. Because the whole half of the face is paralysed, the patient also loses forehead wrinkling and cannot close the eye on that side. Muscle wasting and loss of eye closure are what mark a lower motor neuron lesion, in contrast to the upper motor neuron pattern.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Eye closure is lost, not preserved, because the orbicularis oculi is paralysed.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise muscle wasting and loss of eye closure as features of lower motor neuron facial palsy.

questions.title: Muscle not supplied by the facial nerve
questions.question: Not supplied by the facial nerve:

options.D: Posterior belly of the digastric muscle

explanations.A: Incorrect. The stapedius is supplied by the nerve to stapedius, a branch of the facial nerve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Buccinator is a muscle of facial expression supplied by the facial nerve.
explanations.C: Correct. The levator palpebrae superioris, which raises the upper eyelid, is supplied by the oculomotor nerve (with a sympathetic component), not by the facial nerve. The facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression including buccinator, the stapedius, and the posterior belly of digastric. This is why a facial nerve lesion causes inability to close the eye through orbicularis oculi but does not cause ptosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The posterior belly of the digastric is supplied by the facial nerve.

questions.learning_objective: Recall that levator palpebrae superioris is supplied by the oculomotor, not the facial, nerve.

questions.title: Features of upper motor neuron facial paralysis
questions.question: In upper motor neurone facial paralysis:

options.A: All muscles of the face are affected
options.B: Hypertonia of the muscles is present

explanations.A: Incorrect. The upper face is spared, so not all facial muscles are affected — only the lower face.
explanations.B: Correct. In an upper motor neuron facial palsy the lesion is above the facial nucleus, so the muscles show the features of a pyramidal (spastic) lesion, including hypertonia, and there is no wasting. The upper part of the face, controlling forehead and eye closure, is spared because it has bilateral cortical representation, and emotional (mimetic) movements are often preserved. Only the lower part of the opposite face is weak.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Emotional facial expressions are typically preserved in an upper motor neuron lesion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Muscle wasting is a lower motor neuron feature and does not occur in an upper motor neuron palsy.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that an upper motor neuron facial palsy spares the upper face and shows no wasting.

questions.title: Branches of the facial nerve (the exception)
questions.question: All are branches of the facial nerve EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a branch). The chorda tympani is a branch of the facial nerve carrying taste and secretomotor fibres.
explanations.B: Correct. The greater auricular nerve is a branch of the cervical plexus (from C2 and C3), not of the facial nerve, so it is the exception. The chorda tympani, the nerve to stapedius and the greater superficial petrosal nerve are all genuine branches of the facial nerve. The greater auricular nerve supplies sensation over the parotid and lower ear, which is why it is harvested as a graft but is not part of the facial nerve.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is a branch). The nerve to stapedius arises from the facial nerve in its vertical segment.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is a branch). The greater superficial petrosal nerve leaves the facial nerve at the geniculate ganglion.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish true facial nerve branches from the greater auricular nerve of the cervical plexus.

questions.title: Distribution of lower motor neuron facial paralysis
questions.question: Lower motor neurone facial paralysis affects:

options.A: The upper part of the face
options.B: The lower part of the face
options.C: The whole side of the face

explanations.A: Incorrect. It is not limited to the upper face; the whole side is affected.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Isolated lower-face weakness with forehead sparing is the upper motor neuron pattern, not the lower.
explanations.C: Correct. A lower motor neuron facial palsy interrupts the final common pathway from the facial nucleus, so the entire half of the face on that side is paralysed, involving forehead, eye closure and mouth together. This contrasts with an upper motor neuron lesion, which spares the forehead because of its bilateral cortical supply. Involvement of the whole side, including inability to close the eye, is the hallmark of the lower motor neuron pattern.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The tongue muscles are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve, not the facial nerve.

questions.learning_objective: State that a lower motor neuron facial palsy affects the whole side of the face.

questions.title: Commonest cause of lower motor neuron facial paralysis
questions.question: The most common cause for LMN facial paralysis is:

options.D: As a complication of otitis media

explanations.A: Incorrect. Parotid surgery can injure the nerve but accounts for a small minority of cases.
explanations.B: Correct. Bell's palsy, the idiopathic lower motor neuron facial paralysis, is the single commonest cause of lower motor neuron facial weakness. It is diagnosed once other identifiable causes have been excluded. Parotid or mastoid surgery, trauma and otitis media all cause lower motor neuron palsy but each is far less frequent than Bell's palsy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Trauma is an important cause but much less common than Bell's palsy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Facial palsy complicating otitis media occurs but is uncommon compared with Bell's palsy.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Bell's palsy as the commonest cause of lower motor neuron facial paralysis.

questions.title: Treatment of otosclerosis
questions.question: Treatment of otosclerosis is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Radical mastoidectomy is for cholesteatoma, not for a fixed stapes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Myringoplasty repairs a perforation, but the drum is intact in otosclerosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ventilation tubes treat middle-ear effusion, not stapes fixation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cortical mastoidectomy is for acute mastoid infection, not otosclerosis.
explanations.E: Correct. Otosclerosis fixes the stapes footplate in the oval window, producing a conductive deafness, so the surgical treatment is stapedectomy (or stapedotomy) with insertion of a synthetic piston prosthesis to restore ossicular movement. The alternative for those who decline surgery is a hearing aid. The mastoid and tympanic membrane operations listed are for suppurative disease or perforations, not for a fixed stapes.

questions.learning_objective: State that otosclerosis is treated by stapedectomy with a prosthesis, or a hearing aid.

questions.title: True statements in otosclerosis (the exception)
questions.question: The following are true in otosclerosis except:

options.A: The condition is hereditary and more common in females
options.B: Conductive deafness is due to fixation of stapes footplate
options.C: The stapes is the only ossicle that is involved
options.D: Sensorineural hearing loss never occur in this disease
options.E: Stapedectomy is a good treatment option

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is true). Otosclerosis is hereditary and more common in females.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is true). The conductive deafness results from fixation of the stapes footplate.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is true). The stapes is characteristically the ossicle involved.
explanations.D: Correct. This is the false statement: sensorineural hearing loss can occur in otosclerosis when the otosclerotic focus involves the cochlea (cochlear otosclerosis), so it is wrong to say it never happens. The disease is indeed hereditary, commoner in females and typically causes a conductive deafness from stapes footplate fixation, which stapedectomy treats well. Saying sensorineural loss never occurs is therefore the exception.
explanations.E: Incorrect (this is true). Stapedectomy is a good treatment option.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that otosclerosis may cause sensorineural loss (cochlear otosclerosis), not only conductive.

questions.title: Bilateral conductive hearing loss with family history
questions.question: A 30-year-old female presented by bilateral gradual hearing loss, more in the right ear. Her older sister had the same problem. On examination, a healthy intact tympanic membrane was seen. Rinne test was negative on the right and positive on the left. Weber test was lateralized to the right. The most probable diagnosis is:

explanations.A: Correct. A young woman with bilateral, gradually progressive hearing loss, a positive family history and a normal intact drum, whose tuning-fork tests show a conductive loss (Rinne negative on the right with Weber lateralising to that worse ear), fits otosclerosis. Otosclerosis fixes the stapes to give a conductive loss behind a normal-looking drum and runs in families, commoner in women. The picture is classic for stapedial otosclerosis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ototoxicity causes a sensorineural loss with a positive Rinne, not the conductive pattern seen here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Presbyacusis is age-related sensorineural loss and would not appear at 30 with this family history.
explanations.D: Incorrect. There is no such recognised entity producing this classic conductive familial picture.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A glomus tympanicum gives pulsatile tinnitus and a red retrotympanic mass, not a bilateral familial conductive loss.

questions.learning_objective: Diagnose otosclerosis from bilateral familial conductive loss with a normal drum.

questions.title: Correct statements in otosclerosis (the exception)
questions.question: In otosclerosis, the following is correct except:

options.C: Shows type As curve on tympanometry
options.D: Tympanoplasty in the operation of choice

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is true). Otosclerosis usually affects both ears.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is true). It often progresses during pregnancy.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is true). Tympanometry shows a stiff, shallow type As curve.
explanations.D: Correct. This is the false statement: the operation of choice in otosclerosis is stapedectomy with a prosthesis, not tympanoplasty. Tympanoplasty reconstructs the drum and ossicular chain in chronic ear disease and does not address a fixed stapes footplate. The other statements are true, as otosclerosis is usually bilateral, progresses during pregnancy, shows a shallow type As tympanogram and commonly has a positive family history.
explanations.E: Incorrect (this is true). A positive family history is common.

questions.learning_objective: State that the operation of choice in otosclerosis is stapedectomy, not tympanoplasty.

questions.title: True statements in otosclerosis (the exception on the drum)
questions.question: In Otosclerosis, the following is true except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is true). Otosclerosis usually affects both ears.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is true). It is due to fixation of the stapes footplate.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is true). It commonly causes a conductive hearing loss.
explanations.D: Correct. This is the false statement: in otosclerosis the tympanic membrane is normal in appearance, occasionally showing a pink Schwartze sign over an active focus, not retracted and congested. The disease is bilateral, caused by fixation of the stapes footplate, commonly gives a conductive hearing loss and is commoner in females. A retracted congested drum belongs to middle-ear inflammatory disease, not otosclerosis.
explanations.E: Incorrect (this is true). It is commoner in females.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that the tympanic membrane is normal in otosclerosis, not retracted and congested.

questions.title: Features of otosclerosis (the exception)
questions.question: Otosclerosis is characterized by the following except:

options.D: Treatment is by stapedectomy or hearing aid

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a feature). Otosclerosis characteristically causes a conductive deafness.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is a feature). It typically presents in young adults, including late adolescence.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the exception: otosclerosis is caused by fixation of the stapes footplate, not by Eustachian tube dysfunction, and tube function is normal. It characteristically produces a conductive deafness, presents in young adults, and is treated by stapedectomy or a hearing aid. Eustachian tube dysfunction underlies middle-ear effusion, which is a different condition.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is a feature). Treatment is by stapedectomy or a hearing aid.

questions.learning_objective: State that otosclerosis is stapes fixation, not Eustachian tube dysfunction.

questions.title: A clinical feature of Meniere's disease
questions.question: One of the clinical features of Meniere's disease is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ear discharge indicates middle-ear or external-ear infection, not the sterile inner-ear hydrops of Meniere's.
explanations.B: Correct. Vertigo is one of the cardinal features of Meniere's disease, which is the triad of episodic rotational vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus caused by endolymphatic hydrops. The attacks of vertigo last minutes to hours and are often disabling. Ear discharge, facial paralysis and loss of consciousness are not features of Meniere's disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Facial paralysis is not a feature of Meniere's disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Meniere's causes severe vertigo but not true loss of consciousness.

questions.learning_objective: Identify vertigo as a cardinal clinical feature of Meniere's disease.

questions.title: Features of Meniere's disease (the exception)
questions.question: All of the following are characteristic clinical features of Meniere's disease EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a feature). Fluctuating sensorineural deafness is characteristic of Meniere's disease.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is a feature). Episodic vertigo is a cardinal feature.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is a feature). Tinnitus is part of the Meniere's triad.
explanations.D: Correct. Loss of consciousness is the exception: Meniere's disease never causes true loss of consciousness. Its characteristic features are episodic vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural deafness and tinnitus, and the severe vertigo is commonly accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Fainting or loss of consciousness points to a cardiovascular or neurological cause instead.
explanations.E: Incorrect (this is a feature). Vomiting commonly accompanies the acute vertiginous attack.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that loss of consciousness is not a feature of Meniere's disease.

questions.title: Where endolymphatic hydrops is found
questions.question: Endolymphatic hydrops is found in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Otosclerosis is fixation of the stapes footplate, not endolymphatic hydrops.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chronic suppurative otitis media is a middle-ear infection, unrelated to hydrops.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Wax impaction is a simple external-canal obstruction, not an inner-ear disorder.
explanations.D: Correct. Endolymphatic hydrops, distension of the endolymphatic system of the membranous labyrinth, is the underlying pathology of Meniere's disease. The raised endolymph pressure is thought to produce the episodic vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus. The other conditions listed have quite different mechanisms and do not involve hydrops.

questions.learning_objective: Associate endolymphatic hydrops with Meniere's disease.

questions.title: Management feature of Meniere's disease
questions.question: Meniere's disease is characterized by:

options.A: Attacks of vertigo, tinnitus and conductive hearing loss
options.B: Diuretics are part of the medications prescribed for its management

explanations.A: Incorrect. The hearing loss in Meniere's is sensorineural, not conductive.
explanations.B: Correct. Diuretics, together with salt restriction, are a standard part of the medical management of Meniere's disease, used to reduce endolymph volume and the frequency of attacks. The hearing loss of Meniere's is sensorineural, not conductive; the tympanogram is normal because the middle ear is healthy; and the disease can become bilateral, so it is not strictly unilateral. The only correct statement is that diuretics are used in its management.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The middle ear is normal, so the tympanogram is type A, not type B.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Meniere's disease can become bilateral and is not strictly unilateral.

questions.learning_objective: State that diuretics and salt restriction are part of the medical management of Meniere's disease.

questions.title: Recurrent vertigo, sensorineural loss and tinnitus
questions.question: Recurrent attacks of vertigo, sensori-neural hearing loss and tinnitus is typically characteristic of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Vestibular neuronitis causes vertigo with normal hearing, without the hearing loss and tinnitus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acoustic neuroma gives progressive unilateral hearing loss, not recurrent episodic attacks.
explanations.C: Correct. Recurrent episodic attacks combining vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus are the defining triad of Meniere's disease, caused by endolymphatic hydrops. The episodic, recurrent nature with all three symptoms together is what distinguishes it. Vestibular neuronitis lacks the hearing loss, and an acoustic neuroma gives steady progressive rather than episodic fluctuating symptoms.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Congenital cholesteatoma is a middle-ear keratin sac, not a cause of this vestibular triad.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the recurrent triad of vertigo, sensorineural loss and tinnitus as Meniere's disease.

questions.title: Vertigo without deafness
questions.question: Vertigo without deafness occurs in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Labyrinthitis affects the whole labyrinth, so it causes vertigo with sensorineural hearing loss.
explanations.B: Correct. Vestibular neuritis inflames only the vestibular nerve, producing acute vertigo while hearing is preserved, so vertigo without deafness points to it. Labyrinthitis and Meniere’s disease both involve the cochlea and therefore cause hearing loss with the vertigo. The presence or absence of hearing loss is the key discriminator, and normal hearing localises the problem to the vestibular nerve.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Otosclerosis causes a conductive hearing loss, not isolated vertigo.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Meniere's disease causes vertigo accompanied by fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute vertigo without hearing loss to vestibular neuritis.

questions.title: The triad of Meniere's disease
questions.question: Meniere's disease is characterized by:

options.B: Sensorineural deafness, pain in the ear and tinnitus
options.D: Conductive deafness, facial paralysis and vertigo

explanations.A: Incorrect. The deafness is sensorineural, not conductive, and there is no otorrhoea.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ear pain is not a feature of Meniere's disease.
explanations.C: Correct. Meniere's disease is the triad of sensorineural deafness, tinnitus and vertigo, arising from endolymphatic hydrops of the inner ear. The deafness is sensorineural rather than conductive and it fluctuates, and there is no ear discharge, ear pain or facial paralysis. Only the combination of sensorineural deafness, tinnitus and vertigo describes it correctly.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The deafness is sensorineural and facial paralysis is not a feature.

questions.learning_objective: State the Meniere's triad of sensorineural deafness, tinnitus and vertigo.

questions.title: Symptoms of Meniere's disease (the exception)
questions.question: The following are symptoms of Meniere’s disease except:

explanations.A: Correct. A fainting attack (syncope) is the exception: Meniere's disease does not cause loss of consciousness or fainting. Its symptoms are acute recurrent attacks of vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus. Fainting implies a cardiovascular or neurological cause and is not part of the Meniere's picture.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is a symptom). Acute recurrent attacks of vertigo are characteristic.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is a symptom). Fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss occurs.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is a symptom). Tinnitus is part of the triad.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that fainting is not a symptom of Meniere's disease.

questions.title: Complication of ear syringing
questions.question: One of the complications of ear wash is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Meningitis is a complication of suppurative ear disease, not of syringing a wax-filled canal.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A Bezold abscess is a complication of acute mastoiditis, not of ear washing.
explanations.C: Correct. Forceful ear syringing can rupture the tympanic membrane, causing sudden pain and deafness. A ruptured drum is the classic complication of ear wash. It is avoided by using warm water at low pressure and never syringing a suspected perforation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Otosclerosis is a hereditary fixation of the stapes, unrelated to ear syringing.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise tympanic membrane perforation as a complication of ear syringing.

questions.title: Indication for ear syringing
questions.question: Indications of ear wash include:

options.D: Vegetable foreign body in the ear canal

explanations.A: Correct. Impacted wax is the main indication for ear syringing. Warm water floats the softened wax out of the canal. A glomus tumour, a traumatic perforation and a vegetable foreign body are not indications.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A glomus jugulare tumour is a vascular middle-ear tumour and is not approached by ear washing.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A tympanic membrane perforation is a contraindication, because syringing drives water into the middle ear.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A vegetable (organic) foreign body swells with water and becomes more impacted, so it must not be syringed.

questions.learning_objective: State impacted wax as a main indication for ear syringing.

questions.title: Sudden symptoms after ear syringing
questions.question: After an ear wash was done for a 33-year-old male patient, he suffered sudden severe pain, deafness and felt water in his throat. He might have:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Otomycosis causes itching and canal debris, not sudden pain with water reaching the throat.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acute otitis externa causes pain and tenderness but does not let syringed water pass to the throat.
explanations.C: Correct. Sudden severe pain and deafness with water felt in the throat mean the syringing has perforated the drum. The water has passed through the perforation and Eustachian tube to the nasopharynx. This is the classic presentation of a syringing-induced tympanic membrane perforation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A glomus jugulare tumour presents with pulsatile tinnitus and a conductive loss, not acute pain after syringing.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute sudden pain, deafness and water in the throat after syringing to a tympanic membrane perforation.

questions.title: Ear syringing indications (the exception)
questions.question: Indications for ear wash include all of the following except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is an indication). Wax is the classic indication for ear syringing.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is an indication). A small non-impacted inorganic foreign body can be floated out by syringing.
explanations.C: Correct. A vegetable (organic) foreign body is the exception. It absorbs water and swells, becoming more impacted. For this reason an organic foreign body must not be syringed but removed with instruments.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is an indication). A fungal mass can be washed out as part of aural toilet.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a vegetable foreign body as the contraindication among indications for ear syringing.

questions.hold: The p20 grid keys this A (acute otitis media). Acute otitis media is indeed not an indication for ear syringing, but option D (caloric test) is a caloric-test irrigation of the ear that is itself performed by ear washing, so it is an equally defensible EXCEPT; the item has two non-indications and the key is not uniquely correct. Held per the never-guess rule.

questions.title: Weber test in left middle-ear effusion
questions.question: In a left middle ear effusion, the Weber test will be:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The Weber test is centralised only when hearing is symmetrical; a unilateral effusion makes it lateralise.
explanations.B: Incorrect. It would lateralise to the right only if the right ear had the conductive loss or the left had a sensorineural loss.
explanations.C: Correct. A middle-ear effusion is a conductive hearing loss. In a conductive loss the Weber test lateralises to the diseased ear, which here is the left. It lateralises this way because the affected ear is less distracted by ambient air-conducted sound.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Reduced positive" describes a Rinne response, not a Weber result.

questions.learning_objective: State that in a unilateral conductive loss the Weber test lateralises to the affected ear.

questions.title: Rinne test in secretory otitis media
questions.question: In secretory otitis media the Rinne test is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A positive Rinne (air better than bone) occurs in normal hearing or sensorineural loss, not in the conductive loss of secretory otitis media.
explanations.B: Correct. Secretory otitis media is a conductive hearing loss. The Rinne test is therefore negative, with bone conduction better than air conduction in the affected ear. A negative Rinne is the hallmark of a conductive loss.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Centralised" describes the Weber, not the Rinne, test.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The Rinne test gives a definite negative result here.

questions.learning_objective: State that secretory otitis media gives a negative Rinne test.

questions.hold: The p20 grid keys this A (otosclerosis). A negative Rinne indicates conductive loss, and options A (otosclerosis), B (chronic suppurative otitis media) and C (wax impaction) are all conductive losses that give a negative Rinne, so the key is non-unique and only acoustic neuroma (D, sensorineural) is truly excluded. Multi-answer stem; held per the never-guess rule.

questions.title: Cause of watery ear discharge
questions.question: Watery ear discharge may be due to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Otomycosis produces damp fungal debris, not a clear watery discharge.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bullous myringitis causes painful blood-filled blebs on the drum, not watery otorrhoea.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acute otitis media gives a mucopurulent discharge once the drum ruptures, not clear watery fluid.
explanations.D: Correct. A clear watery ear discharge, especially one that increases on straining, is cerebrospinal fluid otorrhoea. It results from a breach of the dura and temporal bone. Recognising it matters because it carries a risk of meningitis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify cerebrospinal fluid otorrhoea as a cause of clear watery ear discharge.

questions.title: Conductive loss is not a feature of (the exception)
questions.question: Conductive hearing loss is not a feature of:

options.D: Traumatic perforation of the ear drum

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chronic suppurative otitis media damages the drum and ossicles, giving a conductive loss.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Adhesive otitis media fixes the ossicular chain, giving a conductive loss.
explanations.C: Correct. Serous labyrinthitis is an inner-ear disorder. It causes a sensorineural loss with vertigo, not a conductive loss. It is therefore the condition in which conductive loss is not a feature.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A traumatic drum perforation interrupts sound conduction, giving a conductive loss.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise labyrinthitis as causing sensorineural, not conductive, hearing loss.

questions.title: Cause of referred otalgia
questions.question: Referred otalgia occurs in cases of:

options.A: Traumatic perforation of the tympanic membrane

explanations.A: Incorrect. A traumatic perforation causes local (primary) ear pain, not referred pain.
explanations.B: Correct. The temporomandibular joint shares sensory innervation with the ear. Its arthritis therefore causes referred otalgia, with a normal ear examination. Referred otalgia should be suspected whenever ear pain occurs with a normal-looking ear.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Myringitis is inflammation of the drum itself and causes local otalgia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Secretory otitis media causes hearing loss and at most local aural fullness, not referred pain.

questions.learning_objective: Identify temporomandibular joint arthritis as a cause of referred otalgia.

questions.title: Commonest cause of conductive loss in adults
questions.question: The commonest cause of conductive hearing loss in adults is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Otosclerosis is the commonest cause of progressive conductive loss with an intact drum, but it is less common overall than wax.
explanations.B: Correct. Impacted wax is the commonest cause of conductive hearing loss in adults. It is readily reversed simply by removing the wax. Otosclerosis is common too but is less frequent overall than wax.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acute otitis media is commoner in children and is an acute, not the usual adult, cause of conductive loss.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A traumatic drum perforation is an occasional, not the commonest, cause.

questions.learning_objective: State impacted wax as the commonest cause of adult conductive hearing loss.

questions.title: Unilateral sensorineural loss causes (the exception)
questions.question: Unilateral sensorineural hearing loss can be caused by all of the following except:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Mumps is a classic cause of unilateral sensorineural hearing loss.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Meningitis damages the cochlea and causes sensorineural loss.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Labyrinthitis is an inner-ear disorder causing sensorineural loss.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Aminoglycosides are ototoxic and damage the cochlea, causing sensorineural loss.
explanations.E: Correct. Secretory otitis media is a middle-ear effusion that causes a conductive loss. It is therefore the exception among these sensorineural causes. The other four all injure the cochlea or auditory nerve.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish conductive secretory otitis media from causes of sensorineural hearing loss.

questions.title: Causes of deaf-mutism (the exception)
questions.question: Causes of deaf-mutism may be due to all of the following except:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Mumps can cause severe sensorineural deafness leading to deaf-mutism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Meningitis is an important cause of profound childhood sensorineural deafness and deaf-mutism.
explanations.C: Correct. Secretory otitis media causes only a mild reversible conductive loss. It is the exception and does not cause deaf-mutism. Deaf-mutism requires a severe early sensorineural deafness.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ototoxic drugs cause profound sensorineural deafness that can lead to deaf-mutism.

questions.learning_objective: Exclude secretory otitis media as a cause of deaf-mutism.

questions.title: Tuning-fork interpretation: positive Rinne, Weber to the left
questions.question: An adult male has a bilateral positive Rinne test and the Weber test lateralised to the left side. He has:

explanations.A: Correct. A positive Rinne in both ears excludes a conductive loss. The Weber lateralising to the left therefore indicates a sensorineural loss of the opposite, right, ear. In sensorineural loss the Weber shifts towards the better-hearing ear.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A right conductive loss would give a negative Rinne on the right and a Weber lateralised to the right.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A left sensorineural loss would make the Weber lateralise to the better (right) ear, not the left.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A left conductive loss would give a negative Rinne on the left, but the Rinne is positive bilaterally.

questions.learning_objective: Interpret a bilaterally positive Rinne with Weber to one side as a contralateral sensorineural loss.

questions.title: Causes of conductive loss (the exception)
questions.question: The following are causes of conductive hearing loss except:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Otosclerosis fixes the stapes and causes a conductive loss.
explanations.B: Correct. Acoustic (noise) trauma damages the cochlear hair cells. It causes a sensorineural loss and so is the exception here. The other three options all impair middle-ear sound conduction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Otitis media impairs middle-ear sound transmission, causing a conductive loss.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Myringitis inflames the drum and causes a conductive loss.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise acoustic trauma as a sensorineural, not conductive, cause of hearing loss.

questions.title: Conductive loss causes (the exception)
questions.question: Conductive hearing loss may be due to all of the following except:

explanations.A: Correct. Mumps damages the cochlea and causes a sensorineural loss. It is therefore the exception among these conductive causes. Otosclerosis, otitic barotrauma and meatal atresia all give a conductive loss.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Otosclerosis fixes the stapes footplate and causes a conductive loss.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Otitic barotrauma causes middle-ear effusion or haemorrhage, giving a conductive loss.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Meatal atresia blocks sound reaching the drum and causes a conductive loss.

questions.learning_objective: Identify mumps as a sensorineural cause among conductive causes of hearing loss.

questions.title: Myringoplasty definition
questions.question: Myringoplasty means repair of the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Repair of the external ear (pinna) is auriculoplasty, not myringoplasty.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The inner ear is not repaired by myringoplasty.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The Eustachian tube is not the target of myringoplasty.
explanations.D: Correct. Myringoplasty is the surgical repair of the tympanic membrane. A graft is used to close a perforation, without any work on the ossicles. Adding ossicular reconstruction would make it a tympanoplasty.

questions.learning_objective: Define myringoplasty as repair of the tympanic membrane.

questions.title: Indication for myringotomy
questions.question: An indication of myringotomy is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A sensorineural loss is not treated by incising the drum.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A large central perforation already has an opening; it needs repair (myringoplasty), not myringotomy.
explanations.C: Correct. Secretory otitis media that fails medical treatment is drained by myringotomy. A ventilation tube is often inserted at the same time. Draining the effusion restores hearing and ventilates the middle ear.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Otosclerosis is treated by stapedectomy or a hearing aid, not myringotomy.

questions.learning_objective: State secretory otitis media as an indication for myringotomy.

questions.title: Myringotomy — the incorrect statement
questions.question: Which of the following statements is wrong concerning the myringotomy operation:

options.A: It is indicated in acute suppurative otitis media with a bulging drum
options.B: It is indicated in secretory otitis media after failure of medical treatment
options.C: It is better done in the postero-superior quadrant of the tympanic membrane
options.D: Residual perforation of the tympanic membrane is one of its complications

explanations.A: Incorrect (this statement is true). Myringotomy relieves an acute suppurative otitis media with a bulging drum.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this statement is true). It is indicated in secretory otitis media that has failed medical treatment.
explanations.C: Correct (this statement is wrong). Myringotomy is better done in the antero-inferior quadrant. The postero-superior quadrant is avoided because it overlies the ossicles and round window. Incising there risks ossicular and inner-ear injury.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this statement is true). A residual perforation is a recognised complication of myringotomy.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the antero-inferior, not postero-superior, quadrant as the correct site for myringotomy.

questions.title: Definition of radical mastoidectomy
questions.question: By the radical mastoidectomy operation we mean:

options.A: Removal of the mastoid air cells and all middle ear contents except the stapes
options.B: Removal of the diseased mastoid air cells only
options.C: Removal of the mastoid air cells and all middle ear contents with preservation of healthy remnants of the tympanic membrane and ossicles

explanations.A: Correct. Radical mastoidectomy removes the mastoid air cells and all middle-ear contents except the stapes. It exteriorises the cavity into a single space, with no attempt to preserve hearing. Preserving tympanic and ossicular remnants instead would make it the modified radical operation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Removing only the diseased air cells describes a cortical (simple) mastoidectomy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Preserving healthy remnants of the tympanic membrane and ossicles describes the modified radical (Bondy) operation, not the radical one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Option A correctly defines radical mastoidectomy.

questions.learning_objective: Define radical mastoidectomy and distinguish it from cortical and modified radical operations.

questions.title: Treatment of acute mastoiditis
questions.question: Acute mastoiditis is treated by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Radical mastoidectomy is for cholesteatoma (unsafe chronic otitis media), not acute mastoiditis.
explanations.B: Correct. Acute mastoiditis, a coalescent mastoid abscess, is drained by cortical (simple) mastoidectomy. This removes the infected air cells while preserving the middle-ear structures. The radical operation is reserved for cholesteatoma, not for acute mastoiditis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tympanoplasty reconstructs the drum and ossicles in chronic disease; it does not treat acute mastoiditis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Stapedectomy is the operation for otosclerosis.

questions.learning_objective: State cortical mastoidectomy as the treatment of acute mastoiditis.
